say.text: Worked example first. Watch one case walked through in full, then you take over the last steps.
Case one: a sac lies lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. Step 1, the route: lateral means it entered at the deep ring, so it is indirect.
Step 2, the walls: the anterior wall is the external oblique aponeurosis, and the sac runs inside the cord coverings within the canal.

choices.label: I know the canal, skip the walk-through

say.text: Step 3, the cause: this sac came through a patent processus vaginalis, a tube left open from birth, so it is congenital.
Step 4, the picture: it commonly descends into the scrotum and reduces upwards, laterally and backwards.
Now the canal walls, because every sac passes through them.
Which structure reinforces the anterior wall of the canal laterally?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. The anterior wall is the external oblique aponeurosis, reinforced laterally by the internal oblique.
The conjoint tendon lies beside the internal oblique, but it belongs to the posterior wall, not the anterior one.
It tempts because it sits next to the internal oblique in the groin, so it feels like a front reinforcement.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so place the conjoint tendon by the wall it reinforces: posterior, and medially.

say.text: Ask which muscle lies on the front of the canal and reinforces it on its lateral side.
The anterior wall is the external oblique aponeurosis, reinforced laterally by the internal oblique.
The posterior wall is transversalis fascia, reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon.
Case two. A sac bulges forward through the posterior wall, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.
The route is walked for you. Last step: what is the cause of this hernia?

choices.label: Acquired weakness of the posterior wall
A persistent hernial sac from birth
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. A direct sac comes through a posterior wall that has weakened, so its cause is acquired.
A patent processus vaginalis causes an indirect hernia, which follows the cord. This sac comes through the posterior wall, medial to the vessels, so it is not a tube left open.
It tempts because both hernias sit in the same groin, so the congenital label drifts across to the direct one.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate them by cause: a tube open from birth for indirect, a weakened wall for direct.

say.text: A persistent sac from birth describes the indirect hernia, a tube that never closed. This sac is medial to the vessels and comes through the posterior wall.
It tempts because a lump is often assumed to be congenital, so the label is carried to the adult direct sac.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the route first: it tells you whether the sac is the tube or the wall.

say.text: Ask what a direct sac pushes through: a tube that never closed, or a wall that has given way.
A direct sac is acquired. It pushes through the posterior wall, which is transversalis fascia, once that wall weakens.
That wall is reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon. The indirect sac uses a different route: a tube left open, not a weak wall.
Case three. A 3-month-old boy has a right groin swelling that lies lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels and reaches the scrotum.
Which underlying defect explains it?

choices.label: A patent processus vaginalis, open from birth
A weak posterior wall of the canal, acquired
A defect in the transversalis fascia at the triangle
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. A patent processus vaginalis gives a congenital indirect hernia that follows the cord into the scrotum.
A weak posterior wall causes a direct hernia, which arises in adults. A swelling that lies lateral to the vessels comes in at the deep ring, from a tube left open.
It tempts because the canal has a posterior wall, and a weak wall sounds like the usual groin fault.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pair cause with route: a tube open from birth for lateral, a weakened wall for medial.

say.text: A defect at Hesselbach's triangle is the site of a direct hernia, medial to the vessels. This swelling lies lateral, so it entered at the deep ring.
It tempts because the triangle is the groin site people name first, so the swap is easy to make.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so trace the route before the cause: lateral to the vessels points to the deep ring.

say.text: Ask whether this sac follows the cord from birth, or whether a wall has weakened with time.
The processus vaginalis normally closes after the testis descends. If the whole tube stays open, it gives a congenital hernia that reaches the testis.
If only part of it stays open, it gives a funicular hernia that stops above the testis.
So a baby's swelling along the cord is congenital, from a patent processus vaginalis.
Now the triangle. A sac comes through Hesselbach's triangle, so the hernia is direct.
Why does a sac through the triangle count as direct?

choices.label: A weak patch of posterior wall, medial to the vessels
The triangle surrounds the deep ring, so it enters straight in
Its lateral edge is the deep ring, so it skips the canal
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. The triangle is a weak area of the posterior wall, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.
The deep ring is the opening for indirect sacs, lateral to the vessels. It is not inside the triangle, which lies medial to the vessels.
It tempts because the deep ring is the landmark most often named in groin hernias.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so rebuild the triangle from its three sides, and none of them is the deep ring.

say.text: The lateral side of the triangle is the inferior epigastric artery, not the deep ring. A sac in the triangle has not entered the canal at the deep ring.
It tempts because the triangle sits right beside the canal, so the two get merged in memory.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the lateral side: it is a vessel, not a ring.

say.text: Ask which structure sits on the lateral side of the triangle, and where the deep ring lies by comparison.
Hesselbach's triangle has three sides: the inferior epigastric artery laterally, the lateral border of the rectus sheath medially, and the inguinal ligament inferiorly.
A sac pushing through this weak posterior patch is direct, and it lies medial to the vessels.
Older texts and exam keys disagree on the triangle's inferior edge. The original description used one base, and exam keys expect another.
Which is the inferior boundary that exam keys expect?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Exam keys expect the inguinal ligament. The original description used Cooper's ligament as the base.
Cooper's ligament was the original base, so it is the old answer. Exam keys expect the inguinal ligament instead.
It tempts because older texts used it, so it looks like the textbook edge.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so keep the old base and the exam-key base apart: they answer different questions.

say.text: The superficial ring is an opening in the anterior wall, not an edge of the triangle. The triangle's three sides include no ring.
It tempts because the superficial ring is an inguinal landmark that people recall first.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so use the three sides as the test: a ring is never one of them.

say.text: Think about which base the original description used, and which one exam keys expect for the inferior edge.
The original description used Cooper's (pectineal) ligament as the base of the triangle.
Exam keys expect the inguinal ligament as the inferior boundary, so learn that answer, and keep the old base as history.
At laparoscopy a sac sits medial to the inferior epigastric vessels, bulging through the posterior wall.
Which hernia is it?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Medial to the vessels, through the posterior wall, makes it direct, whatever the name suggests.
Indirect is the lateral sac, which enters at the deep ring. This sac lies medial to the vessels, so it has not come in there.
It tempts because indirect sounds like the odd one out, so the label gets pinned on whichever sac looks unusual.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so trace the route, not the word: medial to the vessels points to the posterior wall.

say.text: A femoral hernia sits below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, outside the canal. This sac is medial to the vessels and comes through the posterior wall.
It tempts because both are groin lumps, so the nearest name gets taken.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the two sites: the femoral sits below and lateral to the tubercle, the inguinal above and medial.

say.text: Ask which side of the vessels the sac lies on, and which wall it passes through.
Inguinal hernias are sorted by their route past the inferior epigastric vessels, not by the words direct or indirect.
A sac medial to the vessels that comes through the posterior wall is direct.
Now the clinical picture. Which description fits a direct hernia in an elderly man?
Pick the one that matches its shape, site and reduction.

choices.label: Globular swelling by the tubercle, reduces straight backwards, rarely reaches scrotum
Pear-shaped oblique swelling that usually reaches the scrotum and reduces laterally
Globular swelling near the pubic tubercle that regularly reaches the scrotum
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. A direct hernia is a globular swelling by the tubercle that reduces straight backwards and rarely reaches the scrotum.
This is the indirect hernia: oblique, pear-shaped, and often descending into the scrotum. It is not the direct picture.
It tempts because the scrotal swelling is the most visible sign, so it gets attached to the wrong hernia.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so tie scrotal descent to the cord: it belongs to the indirect hernia.

say.text: A globular swelling by the tubercle is the direct hernia, but a direct hernia rarely reaches the scrotum. Regular descent is the indirect pattern.
It tempts because the site and shape fit, so the scrotal detail seems harmless to add.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so keep the shape and site but drop the scrotum: a direct hernia rarely descends.

say.text: Ask which hernia follows the cord down into the scrotum, and which stays near the pubic tubercle.
An indirect hernia follows the cord, so it commonly descends into the scrotum and reduces upwards, laterally and backwards.
A direct hernia is globular by the tubercle, reduces straight backwards, and rarely descends.
